name: ETAP
subcategory: electrical power system modeling and simulation
tagline: Desktop suite for modeling, simulating and analyzing electrical power systems, from load flow and short circuit to arc flash and protective device coordination.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. ETAP is quoted per module and per license, not published as a monthly number.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely write you a Newton-Raphson load flow solver and an SVG one-line diagram editor in an afternoon, and it will give plausible numbers for a toy radial feeder. What it cannot give you is the thing engineers are actually buying: solvers validated against IEEE and IEC standards, a device library with real manufacturer impedances and relay curves, and the institutional confidence that lets someone stamp a drawing and accept liability for it. Arc flash incident energy per IEEE 1584, protection coordination, transient stability and harmonic analysis are each a research project, not a feature. If your calculation ends up in a permit package or an insurance file, a homemade solver is worse than useless because it is confidently wrong. Build the toy to learn the math, not to replace the license.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you draw a small radial one-line diagram, enter bus and line and load parameters, and run an iterative AC load flow plus a symmetrical three-phase short circuit calculation with printable results.
requirements: Willingness to hand-enter every cable, transformer and machine parameter
Enough power systems knowledge to know when the output is nonsense
whatYouLose: Solvers validated against IEEE and IEC standards, which is the entire basis for trusting a result
Equipment libraries: real transformer impedances, cable ampacities, motor curves, manufacturer relay and fuse characteristics
Arc flash incident energy and PPE category per IEEE 1584, plus protective device coordination plots
Unbalanced, transient stability, motor starting, harmonic and reliability studies
Reports that a reviewing authority, utility or insurer will actually accept
Interoperability with the CAD, SCADA and digital twin workflows a utility or plant already runs on
moatNotes: The software is the delivery mechanism; the product is defensible numbers. Regulators, utilities and insurers effectively name the tools they trust, which makes the vendor list a soft standard.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody buys ETAP because the UI is delightful. They buy it because a load flow or arc flash study is a legal artifact with a name on it, and the accepted way to produce one is a tool whose solvers have been benchmarked, versioned and argued over for decades, with a device library that matches what is physically bolted to the wall. The cost of a wrong answer is a burned switchgear cubicle or a hurt electrician, so the license fee rounds to zero against the liability. Add that big plants and utilities have thousands of existing model files, trained staff and audit history locked to the format, and switching is not a software decision at all.
notes: The solver is a weekend of linear algebra; the credibility is not. The moat is standards compliance plus a device library nobody can reproduce, held in place by the fact that regulators and insurers only accept answers from tools they already know.
prompt:
Build a local-only power system study toy. It is a learning tool, not an engineering tool, and it must say so.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.12, FastAPI, numpy, uvicorn.
- SQLite via plain sqlite3 for saving projects.
- Frontend: one static index.html with vanilla JS and inline SVG. No build step, no npm.

What to build:
1. A one-line diagram editor in SVG: place buses, two-winding transformers, lines/cables, loads, and one source (slack) bus. Drag to move, click to connect, click an element to edit parameters in a side panel.
2. Data model in per-unit with a user-set system MVA base and per-bus kV base. Store R, X, B for branches, MW/MVAr for loads, transformer impedance and tap ratio.
3. Load flow: build the Ybus, solve with Newton-Raphson, full Jacobian, convergence tolerance and max iterations configurable. Report per-bus voltage magnitude and angle, branch flows, branch losses, total system losses, and iteration count.
4. Short circuit: symmetrical three-phase bolted fault at a selected bus using the Zbus method from the positive sequence network. Report fault current in kA and MVA. No asymmetrical, no motor contribution decay, no unbalanced faults.
5. Validation: reject islanded networks, missing slack, zero-impedance branches, and non-convergence with a clear error instead of garbage numbers.
6. Results view with a printable HTML report, plus CSV export of the bus and branch tables.
7. Include two seeded example projects: the IEEE 5-bus classic and a small radial industrial feeder, so results can be sanity-checked against textbook values.

Explicitly out of scope, do not stub or fake:
- Arc flash incident energy, PPE categories, protective device coordination, relay or fuse curves.
- Transient stability, motor starting, harmonics, unbalanced or sequence analysis beyond positive sequence.
- Any manufacturer equipment library. The user types every parameter.

No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. Everything runs on localhost and writes to a local .db file. If you need any config, put it in .env and ship a .env.example.

Put a persistent banner in the UI and a line at the top of every exported report: educational tool, results are not validated against IEEE or IEC standards and must not be used for design, permitting or safety decisions.

Finish with a README containing setup commands, the assumptions baked into the solver, and the known limits.
